summary:
Scientists have used extremely short electrical pulses to explore how much current superconductors can carry. The study appeared in Nature Physics on September 24, 2026. ScienceDaily reported it on October 2.

A superconductor can carry electricity without electrical resistance when it is cold enough. Inside it, electrons form Cooper pairs that work together. But even these materials have a current limit.

Often, tiny magnetic structures called vortices start moving before that deeper limit is reached. Their movement causes resistance and heating. The researchers sent pulses lasting only a few picoseconds through small samples. A picosecond is one trillionth of a second. The pulses were too brief for much vortex movement.

The team tested materials called NbN and YBCO. NbN showed a sharp change after carrying more current than its usual limit. This signaled that Cooper pairs were breaking apart. YBCO weakened more gradually as current increased.

The method gives scientists another way to study the materials' inner behavior. It does not mean superconductors can carry unlimited current. The samples still needed cooling, and the result does not demonstrate superconductivity at room temperature.
title: Tiny Pulses Test Superconductors’ Limits
why_it_matters: Brief pulses help scientists examine behavior that slower effects can hide.
